newsitem.title: FRANCE: French reinsurer Scor posts profit rise.
newsitem.headline: French reinsurer Scor posts profit rise.

text.p: French reinsurer Scor's 1996 earnings matched market expectations and the big difference in profits it reported using U.S. and French accounting methods did not detract from a solid underlying performance, insurance analysts said on Thursday.
"This profit difference doesn't have anything to do with the underlying reinsurance business, which looks fine," one analyst said.

Scor, one of the world's largest providers of reinsurance to property, casualty and life insurers, announced that its 1996 net attributable profit calculated using French accounting methods rocketed 20 percent to 624 million francs.
But according to U.S. GAAP standards, it said its profits rose just 2.2 percent to 705 million francs.

Scor began publishing its results according to U.S. GAAP accounting rules, generally regarded as more transparent, ahead of the listing last year of its shares on Wall Street. But it said it was obliged, under French regulations, to also publish its results using French accounting methods.
A company official attributed the profit difference to the way U.S. and French accounting rules treat such issues, in its case, as capital gains on the sale of treasury stock.

Scor had a capital gain of 29 million francs after tax on sale of treasury stock which it was able to list in its profit and loss account under French rules, but which it had to include in shareholders' equity under U.S. rules, he said.
Scor surprised the market by doubling its net dividend to 10 francs from five and was upbeat about prospects for 1997 even though analysts said the reinsurance cycle was past its peak.
Shares closed up 1.56 percent at 241.0 francs after flinching briefly in midafternoon as Wall Street digested the difference in the French and U.S. earnings results.
"The start of 1997 looks pretty good," Scor chairman Jacques Blondeau told financial analysts. "We don't see any reason why 1997 should be very different from 1996," he said.

Blondeau said that while the industry "had experienced major consolidation and rate pressure in some areas, we have prospered by continuing to expand our global reach and by concentrating on higher margin segments of the reinsurance industry."

He said Scor was "particularly satisfied" by the results of its life reinsurance business. The reinsurer said it aimed to maintain a return on equity according to French accounting rules of between 10 and 12 percent. It stood at 11.3 percent in 1996.

"This is a quality player which has shown consistent profits despite a softening in the reinsurance cycle, thanks to the restructuring of their reinsurance portfolio which has been ongoing since 1993," said an analyst.
